checkpoints: A per-handler try/catch that builds its own JSON error response duplicates work already owned by the framework's centralized error-handling layer (an exception filter on Nest/Spring/ASP.NET, or a central middleware plus recover() on Go) — the entire reason that layer exists is to define ONE response envelope for the whole system.

When every handler catches its own errors, the response shape drifts across endpoints — one returns {message}, another returns {error, detail} — forcing clients to guess the format per endpoint instead of parsing a single contract.

Returning an exception's raw message straight to the client violates hide-by-default: that message belongs to whatever exception fired underneath — a DB driver, an ORM — and can carry table names, column names, or query fragments that must never reach outside the server.

Catching an expected domain error such as "not found" inside a local try/catch collapses it into the same generic response as any other failure, throwing away the information that would let it surface as a real 404 instead of a 500.
Swallowing an error without logging it removes any trace of the failure; when a genuinely unexpected error hits production, there is nothing left to grep for, so observability is effectively gone.

The correct fix is to strip the local try/catch out of the handlers entirely: throw a typed exception (NotFoundException, BadRequestException, or an equivalent typed error/sentinel per stack) for expected cases with a message the domain deliberately chose to expose, and let everything else fall through to the one centralized handler that already classifies, logs, and formats it.

Separating a MUST-FIX (an information leak, lost observability) from a mere style preference matters because the error envelope is a consistency contract every consumer of the API relies on, not a matter of per-handler taste.

The fix can be verified with a test that throws a domain error inside the service, calls the endpoint, asserts the response matches the centralized handler's standard envelope ({statusCode, error, message, timestamp, path}), and asserts the body contains none of the original internal driver or ORM message text.

A single log-heavy endpoint can carry three distinct costs at once — CPU-bound formatting, I/O-bound blocking, and allocation-bound serialization — and each needs to be isolated and measured on its own before any fix is applied, because changing all three together leaves no way to know which one actually mattered.

Colorized, pretty-printed log output (colorize()/nestLike-style formatting) exists for a human reading a terminal during development; in production nobody watches a live terminal, so the service should emit plain single-line structured JSON and push any prettifying work to the reader side — a log viewer or aggregator like Loki/Grafana — instead of spending CPU on it in the request path.

A logging transport that calls a synchronous file-write function (like fs.appendFileSync) on every log call blocks the thread or event loop handling that request until the disk write completes, so a log-heavy endpoint effectively becomes I/O-starved on every request.

The fix for a synchronous file-write transport is to switch to an async or buffered writer, or more simply to drop the homegrown file transport entirely and write to stdout so a collector or sidecar (such as Fluentd or Vector) can ship the logs — either way the service stops waiting on disk.

Logging the full request and response body at info level on every single request is the largest serialization and payload cost of the three, since most successful requests never need their full body to debug; the fix is a level policy that keeps full-body logging only on the error path, sampling a fraction of normal requests, or an allow-list that logs just the handful of fields that matter.

After applying fixes, a before/after load test that re-measures p99 latency and CPU is the only way to confirm the change produced a real improvement, and the same check should verify that log volume hasn't been cut so far that it now hurts debugging.

Every reduction in logging detail trades away some real debugging power, so the honest, sustainable split is to keep full detail on the error path — where an investigation is actually needed — and trim only the happy path, rather than cutting evenly everywhere.
NestJS providers default to singleton scope: one instance is built at bootstrap and shared across every request, which is cheap and sufficient as long as the provider is stateless.

Declaring a provider `Scope.REQUEST` propagates upward through the dependency graph — any provider that depends on it, directly or transitively, is forced into request scope too and loses its singleton lifetime, even if its own code never changed.

In this code, marking `TenantContext` as request-scoped to hold per-request `tenantId` drags `LoggerService` and then `OrderService` into request scope as well, purely because they sit on the chain leading back to it.

The real cost of the regression is not the business logic (`createOrder`'s save call is untouched) but the fact that the entire affected chain of instances now has to be re-constructed and re-resolved on every single request instead of being reused from a shared singleton.

This repeated construction and resolution work is exactly what produces the observed doubling of p99 latency and the 40% throughput drop, since more CPU and allocation work happens per request with no change in what that request actually does.
If a request-scoped provider sits inside the request pipeline itself, such as a guard or interceptor, the same propagation spreads even wider and the performance cost grows correspondingly larger.

The fix is to carry per-request tenant context through an execution-scoped storage mechanism instead of provider scope: AsyncLocalStorage in Node, ThreadLocal in Java, AsyncLocal<T> in C#, or explicit `context.Context` threading in Go all let contextual data travel across async boundaries without making the provider (or anything depending on it) request-scoped, so the whole chain reverts to singleton.

Request scope is genuinely justified only when per-request state absolutely must never leak or mix across requests and no other isolation mechanism exists; using it merely as a convenient way to carry contextual data is what silently propagates reconstruction cost through the dependency graph, as it does here.

Fixing the scope alone is not sufficient proof of resolution — the fix should be validated by re-running the same load profile used to surface the regression and confirming that p99 latency and throughput actually return to baseline, not just that the diff looks cleaner on review.
Interceptors wrap the handler like nested decorators, so each one has an inbound leg that runs before the handler and an outbound leg that runs after it, forming a stack rather than a flat sequence.

On the outbound leg the stack unwinds LIFO: given registration order [A, B], the flow is A.before → B.before → handler → B.after → A.after, so the LATER-registered layer is the one that runs FIRST on the way out.

With registration order [ExecutionTimer, ResponseTransform], ResponseTransform is the later-registered layer, so its outbound logic runs before ExecutionTimer's outbound logic — ResponseTransform reads req.executionMs before ExecutionTimer has written it.

A later-running layer can only read what an earlier-running layer already wrote; when the write happens after the read, the reader sees the value's default or stale state instead of the real one, which is why executionMs comes back null on every request.

Reordering the registration to [ResponseTransform, ExecutionTimer] makes ExecutionTimer the later-registered (and therefore inner) layer, so on the outbound leg its write to req.executionMs happens before ResponseTransform reads and wraps it, fixing the null value.

Registration order controls outbound run order precisely because it determines nesting depth: the interceptor registered later sits closer to the handler and therefore finishes its outbound work first, regardless of the order the interceptors were declared conceptually or intuitively.

Fixing this class of bug is not a matter of trial-and-error swapping — it requires tracing which layer produces a value and which layer consumes it, then placing the producer so it always executes first on the leg where the value is needed.

After reordering, the fix should be confirmed by re-invoking the endpoint and checking that executionMs is now a real number instead of null, and by inspecting logs or traces to confirm the run order matches what is actually being measured, since the chosen order also defines the scope of the measurement (pure handler time versus including the wrapping layer).

On a service declared @Injectable() with no explicit scope, NestJS instantiates it exactly once for the whole application, so any instance field on that service becomes a single box read and written by every request that flows through the app.

Storing per-request data such as requestId as a plain field on a singleton-scoped service is shared mutable state — one instance, one field, many concurrent requests writing to and reading from the same location.

Testing requests one at a time can never surface this bug: the setter writes and the getter reads back-to-back with nothing else executing in between, so the field happens to still hold the correct value by coincidence rather than by correctness.

An `await` inside a request's handler is a suspend point that hands control back to the event loop, and while that request is suspended there, another request's middleware can run and overwrite the exact same shared field before the first request resumes.

Node.js is single-threaded, so this failure is not a multi-threading race — it is an interleaving bug: logically concurrent requests take turns running on one thread, and any await boundary is a window where one request's code can mutate state that another request depends on.

AsyncLocalStorage fixes the problem by creating a fresh, isolated store per request via `als.run()` around the request's entry point, and that store is automatically carried through the entire async call chain, including everything after every `await`.

Reading the per-request value from `als.getStore()` instead of a singleton's instance field means each request's continuation only ever sees its own data, so no amount of async interleaving can let one request read or overwrite another request's requestId.

The fix does not require giving up the shared, app-wide logging pipeline — the middleware, logger, and context service can all remain singleton instances; only the one mutable per-request field is replaced with an isolation mechanism.
